detailed_rationale:
SPARC's FY26 turnaround from heavy losses to a reported profit of Rs 1,55,213 lakhs is, on inspection, entirely a function of one non-recurring event: the sale of a Priority Review Voucher (PRV) for USD 195 million, which contributed Rs 1,84,002 lakhs to 'other operating revenue.' A PRV is a one-time, transferable regulatory asset (awarded by the US FDA and then sold to another pharma company) - it is not a repeatable revenue stream, and total equity only turned positive because of this single monetization event. Strip that out and the picture is much less encouraging: core revenue from contracts/licensing - the actual R&D-partnership business SPARC is meant to be - fell from Rs 7,177 lakhs in FY25 to just Rs 3,915 lakhs in FY26, a genuine decline in the underlying franchise, not growth.

The quant model's 1-year revenue growth figure of roughly 2,510% and growth_1y_score near 99 are a direct, mechanical result of this one-off - the automated scoring has no way to distinguish a one-time asset monetization from organic growth, and taking that score at face value would badly misstate SPARC's trajectory. ROE (-79%) and ROCE (-198%) still reflect the years of accumulated losses this single sale has not erased, and quality_score of just 1.79 - near the floor of the entire universe - is the more honest read of the underlying business health.

Reverse-DCF read: at 5.2x earnings, the market is (correctly, in our view) not extending any credit for the PRV-driven 'profit' - the multiple reflects recognition that this was a balance-sheet event, not an earnings trajectory. On a like-for-like basis, ignoring the one-off, the core contract-research business is shrinking, and there is no visible near-term repeat catalyst of similar scale.
recommendation_rationale: Quant model calls Hold (60.9/69.1), but this rec is being generated in part off a growth score that is itself an artifact of the one-time PRV sale - not something a rescue or downgrade fixes, since the underlying model architecture (not the SPARC-specific inputs) is what's being fooled. We keep the recommendation at Hold ourselves (consistent with the quant call) because the balance sheet is not distressed (D/E 0.42x, interest coverage 47x) and the stock is not being mispriced by the market, but we are escalating the methodology point below.
summary: SPARC's swing from heavy losses to a large reported profit this year came entirely from selling a one-time US FDA Priority Review Voucher for USD 195 million - not from the underlying research and licensing business, which actually shrank year-on-year. This is a one-off balance-sheet event, not a repeatable earnings source, and should not be read as a turnaround in the core franchise. The market's low valuation (about 5 times earnings) appropriately reflects this reality.
positive_para: The PRV sale materially strengthened the balance sheet, turning total equity positive and providing a cash cushion; the company retains standard pharma R&D optionality (regulatory assets/vouchers, licensing deals) that could in principle produce future value events, even if not on a predictable schedule.
negative_para: The core contract/licensing revenue - the actual ongoing business - declined from Rs 71.8cr to Rs 39.2cr year-on-year, a genuine deterioration masked entirely by the one-off voucher sale; ROE and ROCE remain deeply negative, reflecting that years of losses are not resolved by a single asset monetization; there is no disclosed pipeline of similar near-term one-off events to repeat this year's reported profit.
reverse_dcf_judgment: At 5.2x earnings, the market is correctly not crediting the PRV-driven reported profit as a sustainable earnings base - this is a fair, skeptical multiple given that the core licensing business actually contracted this year. We would model forward growth for the recurring business as flat-to-declining, explicitly excluding any assumption of a repeat one-off monetization event, since one is not identified or guaranteed.
escalation_reason: SPARC's FY26 'turnaround' (loss to a Rs 1,552cr profit) and its quant growth score (~99, revenue growth ~2,510% YoY) are entirely attributable to a one-time USD 195mn Priority Review Voucher sale booked as other operating revenue - the actual core contract/licensing business declined YoY (Rs 71.8cr to Rs 39.2cr). This is a case where the automated scoring model has no mechanism to detect that a headline growth/profit swing is a non-recurring asset monetization rather than organic performance, producing a growth score at the ceiling of the model for a business whose real franchise is shrinking. Flagging for the quant/PM team as a potential methodology gap: one-off asset or IP monetization events (PRV sales, land/investment disposals, and similar) could be inflating growth scores at other stocks in the 750-name universe in the same mechanical way, and may warrant a systematic screen (e.g., an 'other operating revenue' or non-recurring-items check against reported revenue growth) rather than relying solely on per-stock analyst catches. I am not changing the recommendation (Hold, matching the quant call) - just flagging the scoring risk for review.
